newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Heavy fighting continues near Colombian capital.
newsitem.headline: Heavy fighting continues near Colombian capital.

text.p: Colombia's army said on Tuesday it was pouring hundreds of reinforcements into a mountainous area outside the capital where at least 19 soldiers and 10 leftist guerrillas have been killed in heavy fighting since the weekend.

Army sources in Villavicencio, capital of Meta province, told Reuters up to 1,000 troops were set to be ferried into the combat zone, about 30 miles (50 km) east of Bogota. They would back up about 400 already in place near the small, deeply impoverished town of San Juanito, where soldiers have been battling hundreds of Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) rebels since Friday.

There were conflicting reports on Tuesday as to the exact toll from the combat, in which troops were backed by helicopter gunships and air force bombers. But Red Cross officials and soldiers in San Juanito told reporters 19 to 21 soliders were killed and at least nine others were missing.

Army commander Gen. Manuel Jose Bonett, who was due to fly into San Juanito on Tuesday, declined to confirm the number of army fatalities, but he and other senior military officials have said at least 10 guerrillas were among the dead in the worst fighting on the outskirts of Bogota in recent memory.

The FARC, Colombia's largest and oldest rebel group, began as a Marxist, pro-Soviet group in 1964. It has grown rich through banditry, kidnapping and the protection of rural drug operations and is believed to have 7,000 to 10,000 recruits.

An international spokesman for the group, in a telephone interview with Reuters from Mexico City, denied that rebels involved in the San Juanito fighting were members of the personal security force of Manuel "Sureshot" Marulanda, the FARC's veteran leader.

But security officials have intercepted radio conversations between the FARC and the International Committee of the Red Cross indicating that Jorge Suarez Briceno, a top FARC military strategist known by his nom de guerre as "Mono Jojoy," was among the rebel leaders directing the combat.

Marulanda, who started fighting in 1948 and was believed to be about 70 years old, maintained his headquarters in Meta province under December 1990, when it was destroyed in an intense campaign of aerial bombardments.

Defence Minister Guillermo Alberto Gonzalez said heavy fighting continued on the outskirts of San Juanito on Tuesday, keeping the government from adding up the dead and injured or issuing an official casualty report.

If the toll of more than 20 soldiers is confirmed, it would be the worst blow to the army since last August when 27 were killed and at least 60 others were taken prisoner by FARC commados who overran a military base in Putumayo province. The soldiers are still being held, along with 10 others who were seized in December in fighting in Choco province.

Bonett last week said Bogota was among the key targets of the FARC and the National Liberation Army, Colombia's No. 2 guerrilla group. But a map of "strategic areas" he told foreign journalists rebels already dominate or hope to seize in the future covered most of Colombia's national territory.
